one: The three main signals from production: logs (events), metrics (numbers over time), traces (one request's path through the system).
an: A car: metrics are the dashboard gauges, logs are the mechanic's notebook, a trace is a GPS recording of one trip with timestamps at each turn.
how: Metrics: cheap aggregated numbers (requests/sec, error rate, p95 latency, CPU). For dashboards and alerts. Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch.
Logs: detailed records of events. For investigating what happened. Should be structured (JSON) and searchable (Loki, ELK, Datadog).
Traces: a tree of timed spans across services for one request. For finding where time went. OpenTelemetry is the standard way to emit all three.
Plus error tracking (Sentry) for grouped exceptions with stack traces and user context.
why: Without them, production is a black box and every incident is guesswork. Seniors set this up before it is needed.
trade: Logs at high volume get expensive fast. High-cardinality metric labels (user IDs) can blow up metric storage. Sample traces.

myth.m: We have logs, so we have observability.
myth.r: Logs tell you what happened once you know where to look. Metrics tell you something is wrong; traces tell you where.

The access log line count
The lockfile

plain:
To understand what production is doing, you collect three kinds of signals. Metrics: numbers over time (requests per second, error rate, response time). Logs: detailed records of individual events. Traces: the path and timing of one request through all your services.

Metrics tell you something is wrong. Traces tell you where. Logs tell you why.
bridge: Sentry in your frontend is error tracking, a close cousin. Vercel/Netlify analytics graphs are metrics. The browser's Network tab waterfall is like a trace for one page load.

walk.title: Investigating “the app is slow” with all three
steps: Metrics dashboard: p95 latency for /checkout jumped from 400ms to 2.5s at 14:10. Other routes are normal.
Open traces for slow checkout requests after 14:10: the inventory-service span went from 50ms to 2s.
Search logs from inventory-service after 14:10: many “lock timeout on table stock” warnings.
A migration deployed at 14:08 is holding a lock on the stock table.
Five minutes from alert to cause, without guessing.

terms: A record of one event, ideally structured (JSON).
One request's timed path across services.
Grouped exceptions with stack traces (e.g. Sentry).
How well you can understand the system from its outputs.
insights: Set these up before you need them. During an outage it is too late to add a metric and wait for data to arrive.
Start small: RED metrics and error tracking on every service first. Add tracing when one request crosses several services or a slow request is hard to explain.
Logs are usually the biggest part of the observability bill, because you pay for every line stored. Metrics stay cheap as long as their labels have a small, fixed set of values.

prod.summary: In production, the three signals are useful only when they connect: a metric spike links to example traces (exemplars), a trace links to the logs of that request (shared trace ID), and all of them use the same service name and environment labels. Seniors standardise on OpenTelemetry for collection, choose one backend per signal, and control cost through cardinality, sampling and retention.
checklist: Every service exposes RED metrics: request rate, error rate and duration histogram, labelled by route template (/orders/:id), method and status class.
Metric labels never contain unbounded values: user ID, email, raw URL, order ID.
Logs include trace_id, so you can jump from a trace to its log lines.
All signals share resource attributes: service.name, service.version, deployment.environment.
Frontend errors and backend errors go to error tracking (Sentry or similar) with release versions and source maps uploaded.
There is a dashboard per service that answers “is it healthy?” in 10 seconds, and each alert links to it.
Retention and sampling are set on purpose: for example metrics 13 months, logs 14–30 days, traces sampled with all errors kept.
numbers: Cardinality is the product of label values: 50 routes × 5 status classes × 4 methods × 30 pods = 30,000 time series for one histogram metric, multiplied again by its bucket count.
prom-client default histogram buckets go from 0.005 to 10 seconds (11 buckets plus +Inf).
OpenTelemetry SDK default sampler is parentbased_always_on: every trace is recorded unless you configure sampling.
failures: Prometheus memory grows until it is OOM-killed; the head series count jumped from 200k to 4M after a deploy.
Cause: someone added userId or the raw URL path as a metric label. Fix: drop the label (relabel rule or code fix), use the route template, and put user IDs in logs and traces instead.
Dashboards show p99 latency is fine, but users complain checkout is slow.

Cause: latency is averaged across all routes, or the histogram buckets top out below the real latency, so slow requests fall into one bucket. Fix: per-route histograms with buckets that cover your real SLO threshold and tail.
During an incident, you find the slow trace but cannot find its logs.
Cause: logs do not include the trace ID, or services use different service names in each tool. Fix: inject trace_id into every log line and align resource attributes.
Sentry shows minified stack traces like at e (main.3f2a.js:1:48213).
Cause: source maps not uploaded for that release. Fix: upload source maps in CI and tag events with the same release name.

code.title: RED metrics with prom-client, labelled by route template
code.note: The route label is where most cardinality explosions start. A histogram gives rate (count), errors (by status_class) and duration (buckets) from one metric.

qs.s: Error rate on /api/orders went from 0.2% to 4% at 10:12. You need to know whether one customer, one pod or everyone is affected. Which order of signals is most efficient?
o: Use metrics to confirm scope (per-pod, per-route error rate), then open traces of failing requests, then read the logs for those trace IDs
Read all logs from 10:00 onward
Profile CPU on each pod
Restart pods one by one and watch the metric
qs.e: Metrics are cheap and aggregated, so they narrow the scope fast. Traces show where in the request it fails; logs with the same trace ID explain why. Reading all logs first does not scale.

qs.s: A developer proposes the label customer_id on http_requests_total so support can see per-customer error rates. You have 200,000 customers. Best response?
o: Fine, Prometheus compresses labels
Put customer ID in logs and trace attributes and query those; per-customer metrics would create hundreds of thousands of series per label combination
Use the label but scrape less often
Hash the customer ID to make it shorter
qs.e: Every distinct label value creates a new time series. Hashing or slower scraping does not reduce the count. High-cardinality detail belongs in logs/traces (or a dedicated analytics store).

qs.s: Average latency for /search is 120 ms. Users still complain it is slow. What is the likely blind spot?
o: The metric is in milliseconds instead of seconds
Search needs logs, not metrics
The average hides the tail; check p95/p99 from a histogram, which may show 5% of searches taking several seconds
Average latency is always correct for user experience
qs.e: If 95% of searches take 50 ms and 5% take 1.5 s, the average is about 120 ms, but 1 in 20 users waits over a second. Percentiles from histograms show this.

qs.s: Read this /metrics output for one route. What share of /search requests took longer than 1 second?

code.title: GET /metrics (excerpt)
code.src:
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/search",le="0.1"} 9100
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/search",le="0.25"} 9400
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/search",le="0.5"} 9500
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/search",le="1"} 9550
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/search",le="2.5"} 9900
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/search",le="+Inf"} 10000
http_request_duration_seconds_count{route="/search"} 10000

o: Cannot tell without the raw logs
qs.e: Prometheus buckets are cumulative: le="1" counts every request up to 1 s (9,550). So 10,000 − 9,550 = 450 requests, 4.5%, were slower. 3.5% is only the 1–2.5 s band (9,900 − 9,550); it forgets the 100 requests above 2.5 s.

qs.s: A teammate adds this middleware. Traffic includes search pages with query strings like /search?q=…. What will you see after a week?

code.title: metrics.ts

o: Nothing unusual; counters are cheap whatever the labels are
Wrong numbers, because status should be a string
Millions of time series, one per unique URL with its query string, until Prometheus memory and query time explode
Only the first 100 paths are kept, because prom-client limits label values
qs.e: originalUrl includes IDs and query strings, so every new search creates a new series in the app's memory and in Prometheus. prom-client has no built-in limit. Use the route template (req.route.path) and drop the query string. The status number is converted to a string, so that is not the problem.

qs.s: A p99 latency panel spikes at 14:20. You want to open one real trace from the slow requests in that spike, not search by time. What connects a metric point to a trace?
o: Add trace_id as a label on the histogram
Search all logs between 14:19 and 14:21
Set trace sampling to 100% for an hour
Exemplars: the histogram stores a sample trace ID with some observations, and Grafana shows them as dots you can click
qs.e: Exemplars attach a trace ID to individual observations without making it a label, so cardinality stays flat. A trace_id label would create a new series for every request: the worst cardinality mistake possible. Exemplars need the OpenMetrics format and a backend that stores them.

qs.s: Logs are 70% of your observability bill. Most of the volume is one line per successful request: {msg: "request completed", route, status, ms}. Which change cuts cost most while keeping the ability to debug?
o: Turn the success line into metrics (a counter and a duration histogram per route), sample or drop success logs, and keep every warn/error line with its trace ID
Delete all logs and rely only on metrics
Keep everything, but shorten retention from 30 days to 2 days
Gzip the logs before shipping
qs.e: Per-request success lines mostly answer aggregate questions (rate, latency), which metrics answer for a tiny fraction of the cost. Errors keep full detail. Two days of retention breaks investigations of anything found late, and compression is usually done by the store already, so it barely changes the bill.

interview.q: You are launching a new backend service next month. What observability do you put in place before the first user arrives?
answer: RED metrics per route template (rate, errors, duration histogram) plus runtime metrics (event loop lag, heap, GC), and USE metrics for the database and queues.
Structured JSON logs to stdout with request ID and trace ID on every line, redaction configured and tested.
OpenTelemetry tracing with context propagation through HTTP and queues, parent-based head sampling, and errors recorded on spans.
Error tracking with release tags and source maps, so a new deploy's errors are visible in minutes.
One SLO on the main user journey, a burn-rate page, an external uptime check, and a 10-second “is it healthy?” dashboard.
Trade-off: start with defaults and few custom metrics; add detail when a real question cannot be answered, not before.
followups: Which of these would you skip if you had only two days?
How do you stop one team from adding a high-cardinality label later?

interview.q: When do you reach for logs, metrics and traces, and how do you connect them during an investigation?
answer: Metrics first: cheap, aggregated, good for detection and scope (which route, which pod, since when).
Traces next: for one slow or failing request, show which hop or query took the time or threw.
Logs last: the detailed “why” for that request, found by trace ID, not by guessing time ranges.
Connections: exemplars from metric to trace, trace_id in every log line, and the same service.name and environment labels in every tool.
Each signal has a different cost model: metrics scale with series count, logs and traces with request volume.
followups: What is an exemplar and what does it need to work?
Where does error tracking like Sentry fit?

interview.q: Your observability bill doubled in a quarter. How do you reduce it without going blind?
answer: Measure first: cost per signal and per service, top metric names by series count, top log sources by bytes.
Metrics: remove unbounded labels, drop unused metrics with relabel rules, reduce histogram buckets where nobody reads them.
Logs: drop health-check and static-file lines, sample success logs, turn high-volume lines into metrics, shorten retention for debug-level data.
Traces: ratio head sampling plus tail sampling that keeps all errors and slow traces.
Prevent regressions: per-service budgets, alerts on series count and log volume, and review of new log lines and labels in code review.
followups: Which of these changes could hide the next incident?
How would you find which label caused a series explosion?

one: Logging key-value data (usually JSON) instead of free text, with a request ID on every line.
an: Filling in a form instead of writing a diary entry. You can search and count forms; diaries need to be read.
how: {"level":"error","msg":"payment failed","orderId":42,"provider":"octo","requestId":"r-9f2","ms":3012}
A correlation / request ID is generated at the edge and passed through every service and log line, so you can pull all logs for one request.
Levels: debug, info, warn, error. Production usually runs at info.
why: "Show all failed payments for provider X in the last hour, grouped by error" becomes one query.
trade: Never log secrets or personal data: passwords, tokens, full card numbers, OTP codes. Logs are widely accessible and kept a long time. Redact at the logger.

myth.r: Unstructured strings without request IDs are nearly unsearchable at scale.

q.s: Which should never be in logs?
o: Order ID
Request ID
The user's OTP code and auth token
Response time in ms
q.e: Anyone with log access could take over accounts. Redact credentials and sensitive personal data.

Configure pino redaction for password, token and authorization paths and prove they are hidden.

plain:
Structured logging means writing logs as data (usually JSON with named fields) instead of free sentences. Then you can search and count them: “all failed payments for provider X in the last hour”.

Every log line should include a request ID, so you can gather every line about one request.
bridge: console.log('payment failed for order ' + id) is a sentence. logger.error({ orderId: id, provider: 'octo' }, 'payment failed') is structured: you can filter by orderId later.

walk.title: Answering a support ticket with logs
steps: Support: “Customer says payment failed at about 3pm, order 812.”
Search logs: orderId = 812. One line: {level: 'error', msg: 'payment failed', requestId: 'r-9f2', provider: 'octo', code: 'card_declined'}.
Search requestId = r-9f2: you see the whole request: cart loaded, tax calculated, provider called, provider declined.
The card was declined by the bank, not a bug.
Support answers in two minutes. With unstructured logs, this could take an hour.

terms: A log line with named fields, usually JSON.
debug / info / warn / error: how important the line is.
A unique ID attached to everything about one request.
Hiding sensitive fields before they are written.
insights: Treat the log schema like an API. Other teams build queries, dashboards and alerts on your field names, so renaming a field silently breaks them.
Log decisions and outcomes (“payment failed, card_declined”), not every step of the code path.
pino is fast because it only writes JSON. Pretty, coloured output (pino-pretty) is for local development, not for production.

prod.summary: In production, logs are JSON lines written to stdout and shipped by an agent (Fluent Bit, Vector, the OpenTelemetry Collector) to a store such as Loki, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, CloudWatch or Datadog. Seniors care about a stable field schema, a request/trace ID on every line, redaction at the logger, and cost: logs are usually the biggest observability bill.
checklist: Logs go to stdout as one JSON object per line; the app does not write or rotate log files itself in containers.
Every line carries requestId and, if tracing is on, trace_id/span_id, set once per request (child logger or AsyncLocalStorage), not passed by hand.
Field names are consistent across services (userId everywhere, not user_id in one and uid in another), ideally following OpenTelemetry semantic conventions.
Redaction is configured in the logger for passwords, tokens, authorization and cookie headers, OTP codes and card numbers, and there is a test that proves it.
Production level is info; debug can be turned on per service without a redeploy.
Errors are logged once, with the stack, at the boundary that handles them, not at every layer they pass through.
Retention and volume have a budget: high-volume success logs (health checks, static files) are dropped or sampled.
numbers: pino numeric levels: trace 10, debug 20, info 30, warn 40, error 50, fatal 60. Default level is info.
pino redaction replaces values with "[Redacted]" by default; the docs say paths without wildcards add about 2% overhead, while wildcard paths cost much more.
OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet lists session IDs, access tokens, passwords, encryption keys and payment card data among data that should not be logged directly.
failures: A security review finds Authorization: Bearer eyJ… in the log store, readable by 60 engineers and kept for a year.
Cause: the HTTP request logger logs all headers. Fix: redact req.headers.authorization and req.headers.cookie in the logger config, purge the affected logs, rotate the exposed tokens.
The logging bill doubles in one month.

Cause: a debug log left in a hot loop, or health-check requests logged every few seconds by every pod. Fix: drop health-check logs at the logger or agent, alert on log volume per service, review new log lines in code review.
You can find the error line, but not the other lines of the same request.

Cause: no request ID, or the ID was lost across a queue or an outbound HTTP call. Fix: create a child logger per request from AsyncLocalStorage, forward the ID (or traceparent) on outbound calls, and put it in job metadata.
Lines from one service are missing in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, and the log shipper reports mapper_parsing_exception.

Cause: services disagree on field types. The first document fixed status as a number (500); another service sends status: "ok", which cannot be parsed as a number, so those documents are rejected and dropped. Fix: a shared logging schema and a shared logger package; put different meanings in different field names (http.status_code vs outcome).
Latency goes up after adding logs; the flame graph shows time in JSON.stringify.
Cause: logging huge objects (full request bodies, ORM entities) on every request. Fix: log selected fields only, use serializers, and avoid wildcard redaction on hot paths.

code.title: pino with redaction and a per-request logger via AsyncLocalStorage
code.note: The child logger adds requestId to every line automatically. Fields go in the first argument and the message second; that order is what keeps the output queryable.

qs.s: This line runs on every request: logger.info(`user ${user.email} paid ${amount}`). What is the best review comment?
o: Fine as it is, it has all the information
Change info to debug and keep the string
Use console.log instead, it is faster
Log structured fields like { userId, amount } instead of an email in a string, so it is searchable and does not leak personal data
qs.e: String interpolation makes the line hard to query, and the email is personal data in a store many people can read. An internal user ID gives the same debugging value with less risk.

qs.s: A Node service logs with requestId, but lines written inside a background job triggered by that request have no ID. What is the most likely reason?
o: pino does not support background jobs
Log levels filter them out
The job runs outside the request's async context (it is queued and picked up later), so the ID must be put in the job payload and restored when the job starts
JSON cannot contain IDs
qs.e: AsyncLocalStorage follows async calls within one execution flow. A queue breaks that flow, so the ID (or trace context) must travel in the job data, the same way traceparent travels in headers.

qs.s: The team wants to log the full request body of every API call “for debugging”. The API handles 3,000 requests per second, with 2 KB bodies on average. What is the main problem?
o: JSON cannot hold request bodies
About 6 MB per second (over 500 GB per day) of logs, much of it personal data, for information you rarely need
Logs are only for errors
pino cannot serialize bodies
qs.e: 3,000 × 2 KB ≈ 6 MB/s ≈ 518 GB/day before indexing overhead. Cost and privacy risk both scale with it. Log selected fields, or capture bodies only for sampled failing requests with redaction.

qs.s: Both lines run in production with pino. Later you search the log store for orderId = 42. What do you find?

code.title: payments.ts
code.src:
logger.info("payment ok", { orderId: 42 });   // line A
logger.info({ orderId: 42 }, "payment ok");   // line B

o: Both lines, because pino merges any object argument into the JSON
Only line B. In line A the object comes after the message, so pino treats it as a format argument; with no %o placeholder it is dropped and the output has no orderId field
Only line A, because the message must come first
Neither, because numbers are not indexed
qs.e: pino's signature is logger.info(mergingObject, message, ...interpolationValues). Arguments after the message are only used for printf-style placeholders. Line A prints {"msg":"payment ok"} with no error and no warning, which is why this bug survives code review. Many other loggers (winston) accept the opposite order, so people bring that habit with them.

qs.s: Support gives you request ID r-77a. Read the logs from two services. Why can you not follow the request into billing?

code.title: logs (orders → billing)

o: Billing logs at the wrong level
The log store indexes each service separately
Orders must log the full response body from billing
Orders does not forward its ID on the outbound call, so billing generates a new one. Fix: send the ID (or traceparent) as a header and have billing reuse an incoming ID instead of creating one
qs.e: A correlation ID only works if every hop passes it on and every receiver reuses it. Here only orderId happens to link the lines, which will not work for requests without an order. OpenTelemetry propagation solves this for trace_id automatically; a custom request ID needs the same treatment.

qs.s: An alert counts level=error lines. After a refactor, it shows four times more errors, but the real failure rate is the same. The code logs the error in the repository, the service, the controller and the global error handler. What is the best fix?
o: Log the error once, at the boundary that handles it (the global handler), and let inner layers add context by wrapping it (new Error("charge failed", { cause: err })) and rethrowing
Change the inner layers to warn
Divide the alert threshold by four
Remove the global error handler
qs.e: “Log and rethrow” in every layer multiplies the lines, cost and noise for one failure. Wrapping with cause keeps the full chain in one log entry. Moving inner logs to warn still duplicates them, and a threshold tuned to duplicates breaks again with the next refactor.

qs.s: During an incident you need debug logs from checkout (40 pods) for 15 minutes. Debug output is about 20 times the info volume. Which approach is best?
o: Set LOG_LEVEL=debug and redeploy all services
Change the level at runtime for that one service (for example a protected admin endpoint or a config flag that sets logger.level), with an automatic switch back after a time limit
Leave production on debug permanently, so it is ready next time
Add console.log lines and hotfix
qs.e: A redeploy takes time and restarts the pods that are showing the problem. Runtime level changes are instant and limited to one service; the automatic revert protects the bill when someone forgets. Permanent debug costs about 20x for data nobody reads.

interview.q: How would you design logging for a group of Node services so that support and engineers can actually use it?
answer: JSON to stdout, one object per line, shipped by an agent (Fluent Bit, Vector, OTel Collector); the app never manages files.
A shared logger package with a fixed schema: service, env, version, requestId, trace_id, consistent field names and types.
Per-request child logger via AsyncLocalStorage, IDs forwarded on outbound calls and in job metadata.
Redaction in the logger with a test; a list of fields that must never be logged.
Levels with meaning: error = someone may need to act; info = business events; debug off in production but switchable at runtime.
Cost control: drop health-check lines, sample success logs, budget per service.
followups: How do you enforce the schema across teams?
Where do you log an error that passes through five layers?

interview.q: A security audit found tokens and emails in your logs. What do you do now, and what do you change so it does not happen again?
answer: Now: rotate the exposed tokens and sessions, limit access to the affected indexes, delete or re-index the data within the retention rules, and check whether this is a reportable personal-data incident.
Find the source: usually a request logger that logs all headers or full bodies, or an error that serializes a whole request object.
Fix at the logger: redact paths for authorization, cookie, passwords, OTPs, card data; prefer allow-lists of fields over deny-lists for request logging.
Prevent: a unit test that logs a fake request and asserts no secret appears; a scanner on the log stream for token patterns; code review rule for new log lines.
Trade-off: allow-lists lose some debugging detail, but a missing field is cheap compared with a leaked token.
followups: Why are deny-lists weaker than allow-lists for redaction?
Is a user ID personal data? Should it be in logs?

interview.q: What is the difference between a request ID and a trace ID? Do you need both?
answer: A request ID is an application-level correlation ID, often from the edge (load balancer or gateway) and shown to support or users.
A trace ID is part of W3C traceparent, created and propagated by OpenTelemetry, and links spans across services.
If tracing is in place, logging trace_id and span_id on every line gives log-to-trace navigation; a separate request ID is then mainly for humans and external systems.
Many teams use the trace ID as the request ID returned in a response header, so there is one ID to search.
Both must survive queues and async jobs, which is the part most often broken.
followups: What happens to the trace ID when a request is not sampled?
How would you return the ID to the frontend for support tickets?

one: Following one request across every service, queue and database call it touches, as a timeline of nested spans.
an: Tracking a parcel through every depot, with arrival and departure times at each. You see exactly where it sat for two days.
how: Each unit of work is a span (name, start, duration, attributes). Spans share a trace ID and point to their parent, forming a tree.
Context propagates via headers (W3C traceparent) between services and via message metadata through queues.
OpenTelemetry instruments common libraries automatically; you send data to Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog, etc.
why: In a system of many services, "why is this slow?" is unanswerable from logs alone. Traces show N+1 queries, sequential calls that could be parallel, and slow dependencies at a glance.
trade: Tracing every request costs storage and some CPU. Head sampling (decide at the start, e.g. keep 10%) is cheap but cannot know yet whether a request will fail or be slow. To keep 10% of normal traffic plus all errors and slow requests you need tail sampling in the OpenTelemetry Collector, which buffers whole traces before deciding and needs all spans of a trace on the same collector.

myth.r: Even a monolith benefits: the trace shows each DB query and external call inside one request.

q.s: A trace shows a request calling 3 independent services one after another, 200ms each. Quick win?
o: Cache DNS
Call them in parallel, cutting ~600ms to ~200ms
Add logs
Shard the DB

Add a manual span around one business function with attributes (orderId).
Make two services call each other and see one trace spanning both.

plain: A trace follows one request through every service, database query and external call it touches, with timing for each step. Each step is a span. Spans nest inside each other, so you see a timeline of exactly where the time went.
bridge: It is the DevTools Network waterfall, but for the backend: instead of seeing which file loaded slowly, you see which database query or service call was slow.

walk.title: Reading one slow trace
steps: Trace for GET /dashboard: total 1.4s.
Span auth: 8ms. Span load user: 12ms.
Spans get orders 400ms, then get messages 400ms, then get stats 400ms, one after another.
They do not depend on each other. Run them in parallel with Promise.all.
Next trace: total 430ms. The trace made the problem visible in seconds.

terms: The full record of one request.
One timed operation within a trace.
The ID shared by all spans of one trace, passed between services in a header.
The standard library and format for traces, metrics and logs.
Keeping only some traces to control cost.
insights: The first trace you open after adding OpenTelemetry often shows an N+1 query or calls that could run in parallel.
A broken trace (two short traces instead of one) almost always means a hop that does not forward traceparent: a queue, a cron job, or a hand-written HTTP client.
Keep span names short and stable. Put IDs in attributes, or the backend cannot group similar spans together.

prod.summary: In production, tracing is usually OpenTelemetry SDKs in each service, exporting OTLP to an OpenTelemetry Collector, which samples and forwards to a backend (Tempo, Jaeger, Honeycomb, Datadog). Seniors check that context propagates through every hop (HTTP, gRPC, queues), that sampling keeps the traces that matter, and that span names and attributes are low-cardinality and useful.
checklist: Instrumentation starts before any library is loaded. For a CommonJS app: node --require ./instrumentation.js app.js. For an ESM app the OpenTelemetry docs also require the loader hook: node --experimental-loader=@opentelemetry/instrumentation/hook.mjs --import ./instrumentation.mjs app.mjs. Without this, libraries are not patched and spans are missing.
traceparent propagates across every boundary, including message queues and background jobs (put it in message headers or job metadata).
Span names are low-cardinality (GET /orders/:id), and details go in attributes (order.id).
Sampling is explicit: parent-based head sampling in SDKs, tail sampling in the Collector for errors and slow traces.
Errors are recorded on spans (recordException + status ERROR) so the backend can find failing traces.
Attributes never contain secrets or full request bodies; SQL statements are recorded without parameter values.
The SDK is shut down on SIGTERM (await sdk.shutdown(), then exit) so the last batch of spans is flushed.
numbers: W3C Trace Context (Recommendation, Nov 2021): traceparent = version (2 hex) – trace-id (32 hex) – parent-id (16 hex) – flags (2 hex), e.g. 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01.
OpenTelemetry SDK defaults: sampler parentbased_always_on, propagators tracecontext,baggage, batch span processor delay 5000 ms, queue 2048 spans, export batch 512, max 128 attributes per span.
OTLP default ports: 4317 (gRPC) and 4318 (HTTP).
Collector tail sampling processor defaults: decision_wait 30s, num_traces 50,000 held in memory.
failures: Each service shows its own short trace; nothing connects the API to the worker that processes the job.
Cause: context is not propagated through the queue. Fix: inject traceparent into message headers when publishing and extract it when consuming (or use a span link for batch consumers).
Traces show only the top HTTP span; no database or Redis spans.

Cause: the SDK started after pg/ioredis were already loaded, or an ESM app was started without the @opentelemetry/instrumentation/hook.mjs loader. Fix: start the SDK first with --require (CommonJS) or the loader hook plus --import (ESM); log the enabled instrumentations at startup and check one trace after every dependency upgrade.
The trace backend bill is huge and the UI is slow.
Cause: default always_on sampling on high-traffic endpoints, plus health checks traced. Fix: ratio-based head sampling, drop health-check spans, and tail-sample to keep errors and slow traces.
Spans are lost during deploys; the last seconds before shutdown never appear.
Cause: the process exits before the batch span processor flushes. Fix: call await sdk.shutdown() in the SIGTERM handler, inside the grace period.
Tail sampling keeps “half” of a trace: the root span but not the downstream spans.
Cause: spans of one trace are spread across several Collector replicas. Fix: a first Collector layer with the loadbalancing exporter routing by trace ID, then tail sampling in the second layer.

code.title: OpenTelemetry setup plus one manual span with error recording
code.note: startActiveSpan makes this span the parent of the HTTP and DB spans created inside it. Forgetting span.end() leaves the span unexported. Adding a SIGTERM listener disables Node's default “exit on SIGTERM”, so the handler must exit itself. paymentProvider stands for your own client.

qs.s: Service A uses head sampling at 10% (parentbased_traceidratio). It calls service B, which is configured with always_on but is parent-based. For a request A decided not to sample, what does B do?
o: B records the trace anyway because it is always_on
B records 10% of those requests
B follows the parent's “not sampled” flag in traceparent and does not record, so traces stay complete or absent, never half
B errors because the configurations differ
qs.e: Parent-based samplers respect the sampled flag in the incoming traceparent. That is why the decision is made once at the root and every service agrees.

qs.s: Your trace shows GET /orders taking 900 ms, with 50 child spans SELECT * FROM items WHERE order_id = $1, each about 15 ms, one after another. What is the problem and fix?
o: Slow network; add a CDN
The database needs more CPU
Too much tracing overhead; lower sampling
An N+1 query pattern; load items for all orders in one query (WHERE order_id = ANY($1)) or a join
qs.e: 50 × 15 ms = 750 ms of the 900 ms is the same query repeated per order. Batching it into one query removes most of the time. Traces make this pattern obvious.

qs.s: You want to keep every trace that has an error or takes over 2 seconds, plus 5% of the rest. Where do you implement this?
o: In the Collector with tail sampling, because the outcome is only known after the trace finishes
In each SDK with a 5% ratio sampler
In the browser with a header
In the database, by logging slow queries
qs.e: A head sampler decides at the first span, before any error or latency is known. Tail sampling buffers the whole trace (default decision_wait 30s) and then applies error, latency and probabilistic policies.

qs.s: Service A calls service B with this header. B uses the default parent-based sampler. B's trace view has nothing for this request, although B's logs show it was handled. Why?

code.title: Outgoing request from A
code.src:
POST /charges HTTP/1.1
Host: billing.internal
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-00
content-type: application/json

o: The trace ID is invalid because it is all lower case
The parent span ID 00f067aa0ba902b7 belongs to A, so B cannot use it
Version 00 means tracing is disabled
The last field 00 is the trace flags: the sampled bit is 0, so A decided not to record this trace and B follows that decision
qs.e: traceparent = version – trace-id (32 hex) – parent-id (16 hex) – flags. Flags 01 means sampled. A parent-based sampler follows the parent's choice, so the trace is absent everywhere, not half-present. Version 00 is simply the current format version; lower-case hex is required by the spec.

qs.s: Find the bug. Some “checkout” spans never appear in the backend, and their child HTTP spans show up with a missing parent.

code.title: checkout.ts

o: The empty-cart return and any exception from charge skip span.end(), so the span is never exported; end it in a finally block
startActiveSpan cannot take an async callback
The span name must include the cart ID
span.end() must be called before await
qs.e: Only ended spans are exported. An early return or a throw leaves this one open forever, so children reference a parent the backend never receives. Async callbacks are supported, and ending before the await would make the span too short to be useful.

qs.s: A queue worker creates its span like this. In the trace UI, every job is a separate trace that does not connect to the API request that queued it. What is the fix?

code.title: worker.ts

o: Use the same tracer name in the API and the worker
Give the span the same name as the API span
When enqueuing, inject the context into the job (propagation.inject(context.active(), job.headers)); in the worker, extract it and start the span with that context as parent (or as a span link)
Increase the sampling rate in the worker
qs.e: Context crosses HTTP automatically because instrumentation reads and writes headers. A custom queue has no headers unless you add them, so the worker starts a new root span. Tracer names and span names do not link spans; only trace context does. For batch consumers that process many messages at once, span links are the usual choice.

qs.s: A service names its spans GET /orders/9312, GET /orders/9313 and so on. The backend generates RED metrics from spans (span metrics). What happens?
o: Nothing, span names are free text
Every order ID creates a new span name and so new metric series; grouping by endpoint becomes useless. Name it GET /orders/:id and put the ID in an order.id attribute
Traces are rejected because names cannot contain digits
Sampling drops spans with long names
qs.e: OpenTelemetry semantic conventions ask for low-cardinality span names (HTTP server spans use the route template) because backends group, index and build metrics by name. The ID is still searchable as an attribute.

interview.q: Walk me through how one trace ID gets from the browser to a database query in a service three hops away.
answer: The first instrumented component without an incoming context (browser SDK, edge or API gateway) starts a root span and creates a 128-bit trace ID.
Each outgoing HTTP or gRPC call injects W3C traceparent (trace ID, parent span ID, sampled flag); the receiver's instrumentation extracts it and makes new spans children of it.
Inside a Node process, context flows through await via AsyncLocalStorage, so DB client spans attach to the active span automatically.
Queues and jobs need manual inject/extract into message headers, or span links for batches.
The sampled flag travels with it, so all services make the same keep/drop decision.
followups: What breaks if one service in the middle is not instrumented?
Would you accept traceparent from the public internet? Why or why not?

interview.q: You handle 20,000 requests per second. Design trace sampling.
answer: SDKs: parent-based ratio sampling (for example 1–10%) so cost is predictable and decisions are consistent across services.
Collector: tail sampling to keep all errors, all traces over the latency SLO threshold, and a small probabilistic share of the rest.
Tail sampling needs all spans of a trace on one Collector: a load-balancing exporter layer routes by trace ID; size memory for num_traces and decision_wait.
Drop noise early: health checks, readiness probes, metrics scrapes.
Trade-off: head sampling is cheap but blind to outcome; tail sampling sees the outcome but costs memory and a stateful tier. Metrics stay unsampled, so rates and SLOs are not affected.
followups: If you head-sample at 1%, can tail sampling still keep all errors?
How do you compute accurate request counts from sampled traces?

interview.q: You added OpenTelemetry, but traces are broken into pieces and some spans are missing. How do you debug it?
answer: Check startup order: is the SDK loaded before the libraries (--require, or the loader hook plus --import for ESM)? Log enabled instrumentations.
Check propagation at each hop: capture the outgoing and incoming headers; is traceparent present and are propagators configured the same (for example W3C vs B3)?
Look for context loss: callbacks or libraries that break AsyncLocalStorage, custom queues without inject/extract.
Check export: spans not ended, process exiting before flush, exporter errors, Collector dropping data (its own metrics show refused/dropped spans).
Check sampling: parent sampled flag, tail sampling spread across Collector replicas.
followups: What Collector metrics would you look at first?
How would you test propagation in CI?

one: SLI: a measured signal of user happiness. SLO: the target for it. SLA: a contractual promise with penalties. Error budget: how much failure the SLO allows.
an: SLI is your actual exam score, SLO is the grade you aim for, SLA is the grade written into your scholarship contract.
how: SLI example: % of checkout requests that succeed in under 1s. SLO: 99.9% over 30 days.
99.9% over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of failure. That is the error budget. 99.99% allows about 4 minutes.
If the budget is healthy, ship faster and take risks. If it is burned, slow down and spend effort on reliability. It turns reliability from an argument into a number.
why: "100% uptime" is impossible and chasing it slows everything. SLOs let product and engineering agree how reliable is reliable enough.
trade: Pick SLIs users feel (success, latency) rather than machine stats (CPU). Too many SLOs and nobody watches them.

myth.r: Reliability cost grows very fast: the Google SRE book says one extra increment “may cost 100x more than the previous increment”. And a user on a 99% reliable phone network cannot tell 99.99% from 99.999%.

q.s: An SLO of 99.9% monthly availability allows roughly how much downtime per 30 days?
o: 4 minutes
43 minutes
7 hours
3 days

lab: Pick one user journey of an app you own (e.g. login). Write the SLI as a formula, choose an SLO, and calculate the monthly error budget in minutes and in failed requests at your traffic.
Compute last week's actual SLI from logs or metrics if you have them.
docs: Google SRE book: Service level objectives

plain:
An SLI is a measurement of what users experience, for example “percentage of checkout requests that succeed in under 1 second”. An SLO is your target for it, for example 99.9% per month. An SLA is a promise in a contract, with penalties.

The gap between 100% and the SLO is your error budget: how much failure is acceptable.
bridge: You already think this way about Core Web Vitals: “LCP under 2.5s for 75% of users” is an SLI with a target. SLOs apply the same idea to backend reliability.

walk.title: Using an error budget to decide
steps: SLO: 99.9% of requests succeed each month. With 10 million requests, that allows 10,000 failures.
By the 15th, an incident caused 8,000 failures. 80% of the budget is used.
The team agreed in advance: above 75% budget used, risky launches wait and reliability work comes first.
The big database migration planned for this week moves to next month; the team fixes the cause of the incident instead.
No argument needed: the number made the decision.

terms: Service level indicator: a measured signal of user happiness.
Service level objective: the target for an SLI.
Service level agreement: a contract with consequences.
insights: Start with one or two SLOs for the journeys users care about most (login, checkout), not one per service.
An SLO with no burn-rate alert and no error budget policy is just a chart. The alert and the policy are what make it change behaviour.
Set the first SLO close to what you achieve today, then tighten it if users still complain.

prod.summary: In production, an SLO is only real if it is measured from the user's side, shown on a dashboard people look at, alerted on by burn rate, and backed by an error budget policy that leadership signed. Seniors define the SLI precisely (which requests count, where measured, what is “good”) because a vague SLI produces a number nobody trusts.
checklist: The SLI is a ratio of good events to valid events, written as a formula: for example “HTTP 2xx/3xx/4xx responses under 500 ms ÷ all requests to /api/checkout, excluding health checks”.
It is measured as close to the user as possible (load balancer or client), not only inside the app, which cannot see its own crashes.
Latency SLIs use a threshold on a percentile or on a “fast enough” count, never the average.
The window (usually 30 days rolling) and the target are agreed with product, and are lower than any external SLA.
An error budget policy says what happens when the budget is spent (for example: freeze risky launches, reliability work first) and who can override it.
Alerts use burn rate on the SLO, not raw thresholds.
SLOs are reviewed every quarter: if users complain while the SLO is green, the SLI is measuring the wrong thing.
numbers: 30 days = 43,200 minutes. 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes; 99.95% allows 21.6 minutes; 99.99% allows 4.3 minutes.
At 10 million requests a month, 99.9% allows 10,000 failed requests.
Google SRE book: an incremental improvement in reliability “may cost 100x more than the previous increment”.
Burn rate 1 spends exactly the whole budget in the window; burn rate 14.4 spends 2% of a 30-day budget in 1 hour.
failures: The SLO dashboard is green, but support tickets about “the app not loading” keep coming.

Cause: the SLI is measured inside the app server, so requests that fail at the load balancer, CDN or during pod restarts are invisible. Fix: measure at the edge (load balancer logs, synthetic checks or real-user monitoring).
The team hits 99.99% every month, but feature work is slow and every deploy needs three approvals.

Cause: the system is far more reliable than users need, and nobody spends the budget. Fix: lower process cost (faster deploys, fewer gates) or lower the SLO; unused budget is a signal you could move faster.
Error budget is gone by day 10, but launches continue and nothing changes.
Cause: no agreed error budget policy, so the SLO has no consequence. Fix: write the policy before the next quarter, get it signed by product and engineering leadership.
Latency SLO uses average response time and looks fine; users on slow pages are unhappy.
Cause: averages hide the tail. Fix: SLI = share of requests faster than a threshold (for example 95% under 300 ms), computed from histograms.

code.title: Error budget and burn rate as plain arithmetic
code.note: Burn rate is what makes alerts sensible: 1.44% errors sounds small, but at a 99.9% SLO it empties a 30-day budget in about two days.

qs.s: Your API serves 2 million requests per day. The SLO is 99.95% over 30 days. How many failed requests does the monthly error budget allow?
qs.e: 30 days × 2M = 60M requests. 0.05% of 60M = 30,000. 1,000 is the daily budget at 99.95% (0.05% of 2M); 60,000 would be 99.9%.

qs.s: Which SLI best captures “checkout works” for users?
o: Share of checkout requests, measured at the load balancer, that return a non-5xx response in under 1 second
Average CPU of the checkout pods
Number of checkout pods in Ready state
Average checkout response time measured inside the app
qs.e: A good SLI is a ratio of good events to all events, measured near the user, with a clear “good” rule. Pod counts and CPU are causes; averages hide slow users; in-app timing misses requests the app never received.

qs.s: It is day 12. The 99.9% SLO's 30-day budget is 95% used after two incidents. Product wants to launch a large, risky redesign tomorrow. The error budget policy says: “Over 75% used → only reliability work and low-risk changes.” What is the lead's best move?
o: Launch anyway; the SLO is internal
Lower the SLO to 99% this month so the launch fits
Ask for more servers
Follow the policy: hold the launch, put effort into the incident follow-ups, and escalate if product wants a formal exception
qs.e: The point of a pre-agreed policy is that the number decides, not the loudest voice. Changing the SLO to fit a launch destroys trust in it; exceptions go through the named owner.

qs.s: Read the SLO panel. If failures continue at the same average rate as the first 10 days, when does the error budget run out?

code.title: SLO dashboard, day 10 of 30
code.src:
SLO:               99.9% of requests succeed (30-day window)
Expected traffic:  10,000,000 requests / 30 days
Error budget:      10,000 failed requests
Failed so far:     6,000 (days 1-10)
Budget remaining:  4,000

o: Around day 13
Around day 17
Day 30, exactly on budget
It has already run out
qs.e: 6,000 failures in 10 days is 600 per day. 4,000 remaining ÷ 600 ≈ 6.7 more days, so about day 17. The burn rate is 6,000 ÷ (10,000 × 10/30) = 1.8: faster than budget, which is why the budget ends well before day 30.

qs.s: This SLI query has been green for months while users complain. 40% of all requests to the service are Kubernetes and load balancer health checks. What is wrong?

code.title: SLI recording rule (PromQL)
code.src:
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api", code!~"5.."}[30d]))
/
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[30d]))

o: rate cannot be used over 30 days
4xx responses should be counted as failures
Health checks almost always succeed, so they add many “good” events and dilute real failures; exclude them (filter by route) so the SLI counts only user requests
The query should use avg instead of sum
qs.e: If 40% of events are health checks that always pass, a real failure rate of 0.15% shows as about 0.09%, inside a 99.9% SLO. The SLI must count valid user events only. 4xx is usually the client's fault and counted as good or excluded, and a 30-day rate works, although teams usually precompute shorter windows for speed.

qs.s: Your contract (SLA) promises customers 99.9% monthly availability with service credits. What internal SLO should engineering target?
o: A stricter internal SLO, for example 99.95%, so burn-rate alerts and the budget policy react before the SLA is at risk
Exactly 99.9%, to match the contract
99%, because SLOs are internal and should be relaxed
100%, because there is money involved
qs.e: The SLO is the early warning; the SLA is the penalty line. If they are equal, the first time you miss the SLO you already owe credits. 100% is not reachable and would block all change.

qs.s: A 60-minute full outage happens at 03:00, when traffic is 200 requests per minute. The month has 20 million requests. The SLO is 99.9% over 30 days. Which statement is true?
o: Both a request-based and a time-based SLO are broken
Neither is affected, because night traffic does not count
Request-based: 12,000 failed of a 20,000 budget (60% used, SLO still met). Time-based: 60 bad minutes is more than the 43.2 allowed, so the SLO is broken
Request-based: SLO broken. Time-based: still met
qs.e: 60 × 200 = 12,000 failures; 0.1% of 20M = 20,000. Counting minutes instead, 60 bad minutes exceeds 43.2. Request-based SLIs weigh failures by how many users were hurt; time-based ones treat a quiet hour like a busy one. Neither is wrong, but you must know which one you have.

interview.q: How would you choose SLIs and SLOs for a checkout service?
answer: Start from the user journey: “a customer can pay and gets a confirmation quickly”.
SLIs as ratios of good to valid events: availability (non-5xx at the load balancer, excluding health checks) and latency (share under a threshold, for example 1 s).
Measure close to the user (load balancer or client), and accept that app-only metrics miss crashes and network failures.
Set the target from history and business need, not from wishes: look at the last 3 months, agree with product, keep it below 100% and stricter than any SLA.
Window: 30 days rolling; few SLOs per service so people actually watch them.
Write the error budget policy at the same time, otherwise the SLO has no effect.
followups: Would you count a declined card as a failure?
How do you handle a dependency (payment provider) you do not control?

interview.q: What is an error budget, and how does it change decisions between product and engineering?
answer: Budget = 1 − SLO over the window; for 99.9% and 10M requests, 10,000 failures.
While budget remains, the team may take risk: ship faster, run experiments, do migrations.
When it is spent, the pre-agreed policy applies: freeze risky launches, prioritise reliability work from the postmortems.
It turns “is it reliable enough?” from opinion into a number both sides agreed in advance.
Trade-off: a policy without leadership support is ignored; exceptions must go through a named owner and be recorded.
followups: What do you do if the budget is never used?
Does an outage at a third-party provider spend your budget?

interview.q: Why not alert simply when the SLI drops below the SLO? Explain burn-rate alerting.
answer: A 30-day SLI moves slowly: by the time it crosses the target, the budget is already gone; a short-window threshold, on the other hand, pages on harmless blips.
Burn rate = observed error ratio ÷ allowed error ratio. 1 means the budget lasts exactly the window.
Page on fast burn (14.4 over 1 h, 2% of a 30-day budget) and medium burn (6 over 6 h, 5%); ticket on slow burn (1 over 3 days, 10%).
Pair each long window with a short one (5 min, 30 min) so the alert resets quickly after the fix.
Trade-off: low-traffic services get noisy ratios; use longer windows, minimum request counts or synthetic traffic.
followups: How many hours until the budget is gone at burn rate 14.4?
How would you adapt this for a service with 50 requests per hour?

one: Paging a human only when users are affected and action is needed, based on symptoms rather than causes.
an: A smoke alarm should go off for fire, not every time someone makes toast.
how: Alert on symptoms (error rate up, latency SLO burning fast, checkout success down), not on every cause (CPU 80%) which may be harmless.
Every page needs a runbook: what it means, how to check, how to mitigate. Link it from the alert itself (runbook_url annotation).

Burn-rate alerts: the burn rate is how fast you spend the error budget compared with “exactly on budget”. The Google SRE workbook starting point for a 99.9% SLO: page at burn rate 14.4 over 1 hour (2% of the monthly budget gone), page at 6 over 6 hours (5%), open a ticket at 1 over 3 days (10%).
Each long window is paired with a short one (1h with 5m, 6h with 30m) so the alert stops quickly once the problem is fixed.
why: Alert fatigue is dangerous: teams paged 30 times a night start ignoring pages, then miss the real one.
trade: Too few alerts and users report outages before you notice. Review every page: was it actionable? If not, fix or delete the alert.

myth.r: Noisy alerts get muted. Fewer, high-signal alerts get acted on.

q.s: On-call gets paged nightly for 'CPU > 85%' on a batch worker that finishes fine anyway. Best action?
o: Add a second alert
Remove or downgrade it; alert on job failure or lateness instead
Buy bigger servers
Ignore pages at night
q.e: High CPU on a batch job is normal. Alert on the outcome users care about.

lab: Write three alerts for an app you own: one symptom-based page, one ticket-level warning, and one you decide not to create. Write a 5-line runbook for the page.
Set up an uptime check (Better Stack, UptimeRobot, or Grafana) on a live URL and route it to your phone.
docs: Google SRE workbook: Alerting on SLOs
Rob Ewaschuk: My philosophy on alerting

plain:
Alerting means waking a human only when users are actually affected and someone needs to act. Alert on symptoms (errors are high, checkout is failing) rather than every possible cause (CPU is at 85%), which is often harmless.

Too many alerts are as dangerous as too few: people start ignoring them.
bridge: If you have a Slack channel full of automated warnings that everyone has muted, you have seen alert fatigue.

walk.title: Cleaning up a noisy on-call
steps: On-call gets 25 pages a week. Most say “CPU above 80%” or “disk above 70%” and need no action.
Review each alert: did anyone need to do anything? 20 of 25: no.
Delete or downgrade those to daytime tickets.
Add two symptom alerts: “checkout success below 98% for 5 minutes” and “error budget burning fast”. Each links to a short runbook.
Next month: 3 pages, all real. People respond to them quickly because they trust them again.

terms: An alert that wakes someone up.
What users feel vs a possible reason behind it.
Short instructions: what this alert means and what to do.
Ignoring alerts because most are noise.
insights: Every page should be actionable. If nobody needed to act, delete the alert or make it a ticket.
Write the runbook when you create the alert, not during the incident at 3 a.m.
For a small project, one external uptime check routed to your phone catches most real outages.

prod.summary: In production, alerting is a pipeline: metrics → alert rules (Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch) → a router that groups and silences (Alertmanager, PagerDuty, Opsgenie) → one on-call human. Seniors care about two numbers: how many pages per shift, and what share of pages needed action. Every page must be urgent, user-facing and actionable.
checklist: Every paging alert is tied to a user-facing symptom or an SLO burn rate, not to CPU, memory or disk on one host.
Every alert has a runbook_url and a summary that says which service, which SLO and how bad, so the on-call can act from the phone.
Severity is explicit: page (wake someone) vs ticket (fix during work hours). Most alerts should be tickets.
Alerts are grouped and inhibited: when a whole region is down, on-call gets one page, not 200 (Alertmanager group_by and inhibit_rules).
There is a dead-man's-switch alert (an always-firing “Watchdog”) so you notice when the alerting pipeline itself is broken.
An outside uptime check exists, because if the cluster that runs Prometheus is down, it cannot alert about itself.
Alert quality is reviewed every week or every rotation: delete or downgrade any page that needed no action.
numbers: Google SRE workbook, 99.9% SLO: page at burn rate 14.4 over 1h (2% of budget) and 6 over 6h (5%); ticket at 1 over 3 days (10%).
At burn rate 14.4 a 30-day budget is gone in 720 h ÷ 14.4 = 50 hours.
Alertmanager defaults: group_wait 30s, group_interval 5m, repeat_interval 4h.
Prometheus default scrape_interval and evaluation_interval are both 1 minute, so a rule cannot react faster than about 1–2 minutes plus its for: duration.
failures: On-call gets 40 pages a week and starts acknowledging them without looking. A real outage is missed for 25 minutes.

Cause: cause-based alerts (CPU, disk, single pod restarts) paging at night. Fix: review the last month of pages, delete or downgrade every one that needed no action, and page only on SLO burn and hard user-facing failures.
Users report the site is down on social media; no alert fired.

Cause: alerts only watched internal metrics, and the metrics stack was in the same broken cluster (or the error happened at the CDN/DNS layer before your app). Fix: add an external synthetic check and a Watchdog alert routed outside the cluster.
A 5-minute error spike pages, then resolves by itself before anyone logs in. It happens three times a week.
Cause: threshold alert on a short window with no for: and no multi-window check. Fix: use multi-window burn-rate alerts; short spikes that do not threaten the budget become tickets or nothing.
One database failover produces 300 notifications across Slack and phone.

Cause: every service alerts on its own symptom with no grouping. Fix: group_by: [alertname, cluster], inhibition rules (a “DatabaseDown” alert suppresses dependent “HighErrorRate” alerts), and one incident channel.
The alert fires, but the on-call does not know what the metric means or what to do.
Cause: no runbook, and the alert name is the PromQL expression. Fix: required summary, description and runbook_url annotations, checked in code review.

code.title: Prometheus multi-window burn-rate page for a 99.9% SLO
code.src:
groups:
  - name: checkout-slo
    rules:
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
        # 14.4 x the allowed error ratio (0.1%) over 1h AND over 5m
        expr: |
          (
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",code=~"5.."}[1h]))
            / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[1h]))
          ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
          and
          (
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",code=~"5.."}[5m]))
            / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))
          ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout is burning its 30-day error budget 14x too fast"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/checkout-error-budget"
code.note: The 1h window proves the problem is real; the 5m window makes the alert clear quickly once errors stop. Copy the rule with 6h/30m and factor 6 for the second page, and 3d/6h with factor 1 as a ticket.

qs.s: Your checkout SLO is 99.9% over 30 days. Over the last hour, 1.5% of checkout requests failed, and over the last 5 minutes 1.6% failed. Using the SRE workbook fast-burn rule (burn rate 14.4 on 1h and 5m), what happens?
o: It pages: 1.5% ÷ 0.1% = burn rate 15, which is above 14.4 on both windows
Nothing: 1.5% errors is still under the 2% budget
It opens a ticket, because only the 3-day window can page
It pages only if CPU is also high
qs.e: Burn rate = error ratio ÷ allowed error ratio = 1.5% ÷ 0.1% = 15. Both windows are above 14.4, so the page fires. “2%” in the workbook is the share of the monthly budget spent in 1 hour, not an error-rate threshold.

qs.s: A database goes down. Within two minutes the on-call phone receives 180 separate pages from 30 services. Which change helps most?
o: Lower repeat_interval so pages arrive faster
Remove all database alerts
Increase the Prometheus scrape interval
Group alerts by cluster and add an inhibition rule so “DatabaseDown” suppresses dependent error-rate alerts
qs.e: Grouping and inhibition turn one root problem into one page with context. Removing database alerts loses the most useful signal; scrape interval and repeat interval do not reduce fan-out.

qs.s: Your whole monitoring stack (Prometheus + Alertmanager) runs in the same Kubernetes cluster as the app. The cluster's network fails. What do you see?
o: A flood of pages for every service
One page from Alertmanager about the network
Probably no pages at all, unless you have an external uptime check or a dead-man's-switch watched from outside
Pages delayed by exactly group_wait
qs.e: A monitor cannot report its own death. An outside synthetic check, or a Watchdog alert whose absence is noticed by an external service, covers this blind spot.

qs.s: A database failover produced 300 separate notifications, one per alert. Read the Alertmanager route. Which line is the main cause?

code.title: alertmanager.yml
code.src:
route:
  receiver: oncall-pager
  group_by: ['...']
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
receivers:
  - name: oncall-pager
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: <secret>

o: group_wait: 30s is too short
group_by: ['...'] groups by all labels, so every alert (each pod, each service) is its own group and its own notification
repeat_interval: 4h resends every alert
PagerDuty cannot receive grouped alerts
qs.e: The special value '...' means “group by every label”, which effectively turns grouping off. Grouping by [alertname, cluster] or [cluster, service] plus inhibition rules gives one page with a list. group_wait controls how long to collect the first batch; 30s is the default and fine.

qs.s: Find the problem with this paging rule for a service whose traffic goes from 2,000 requests/s by day to 3 requests/s at night.

code.title: rules.yml
code.src:
- alert: ApiErrors
  expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",code=~"5.."}[5m])) > 5
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: page

o: for: 5m must be longer than the range [5m]
rate must be replaced by increase
The rule is fine; 5 errors per second is always bad

An absolute error count does not scale with traffic: by day 5 errors/s is 0.25% (maybe fine), at night the service could fail 100% of requests (3/s) and never page. Alert on the error ratio, ideally as a burn rate
qs.e: Users feel the share of failed requests, not the count. A ratio (errors ÷ total) works at any traffic level; burn rate ties it to the SLO. At very low traffic, also require a minimum number of requests so one failure does not page. rate vs increase is just per-second vs total; both have the same scaling problem.

qs.s: SLO 99.9% over 30 days. For the last 6 hours the error ratio has been steady at 0.7%. Rules follow the SRE workbook: page at 14.4 (1h and 5m), page at 6 (6h and 30m), ticket at 1 (3d and 6h). What fires?
o: The 6x page (burn rate 7 over 6h and 30m) and the ticket rule; the fast-burn page does not fire because 7 is below 14.4
Only the fast-burn page
Nothing, because 0.7% is below 1%
Only a ticket, because errors are steady
qs.e: Burn rate = 0.7% ÷ 0.1% = 7. That is above 6 and above 1, below 14.4. In those 6 hours about 7 × 6 ÷ 720 ≈ 5.8% of the monthly budget is gone, which is why the slower rule still pages. In practice Alertmanager inhibition often hides the ticket while the page is active.

qs.s: You add an always-firing “Watchdog” alert. How must it be wired to protect you from a dead monitoring stack?
o: Route it to the on-call phone so they see it is alive
Add a second Prometheus in the same cluster that alerts when the first one is down
Alert on up{job="prometheus"} == 0 from the same Prometheus
Route it to an external heartbeat service (dead man's switch) that expects it every few minutes and pages through a separate path when it stops arriving
qs.e: The Watchdog's value is its absence. Only something outside the failure domain can notice that absence. A Prometheus cannot alert that it is down itself, and a second one in the same cluster dies with the cluster. Paging humans with an always-firing alert is pure noise.

interview.q: Design alerting for a new customer-facing API. What pages, what becomes a ticket, and what do you not alert on?
answer: Page: SLO burn-rate alerts (fast and medium burn) on availability and latency, and an external synthetic check of the main journey.
Ticket: slow burn, certificate expiry within 14 days, disk filling within days, backup age, dependency deprecations.
No alert (dashboard only): CPU, memory, single pod restarts, queue depth that does not affect users yet.
Every page has a summary, severity, runbook link and dashboard link; grouping and inhibition so one failure gives one page.
A Watchdog to an external dead man's switch, and an alert review every rotation.
followups: When would you page on a cause instead of a symptom?
How do you alert on a batch job that runs once a night?

interview.q: Your on-call gets 50 pages a week and people are burning out. What do you do in the first month?
answer: Get data: export last month's pages, mark each one actionable or not, and who did what.
Delete or downgrade every non-actionable page to a ticket or dashboard; fix flapping thresholds with for: or burn-rate windows.
Group and inhibit: find storms where one root cause produced many pages.
Add missing symptom alerts so removing noise does not reduce coverage.
Set a target (for example, at most 2 pages per shift) and review in each handoff; protect the on-call's time for fixing the causes.
Trade-off: some risk of missing something during cleanup; the external uptime check and SLO alerts are the safety net.
followups: How do you convince a team that wants to keep its CPU alerts?
What metrics show that on-call health improved?

interview.q: Explain multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts. Why two windows per rule?
answer: Burn rate compares the current error ratio with the ratio the SLO allows.
The long window (1 h, 6 h, 3 d) proves enough budget is really being spent, so short blips do not page.
The short window (5 m, 30 m, 6 h) must also be high, so the alert stops soon after the problem is fixed instead of firing for an hour.
Several rules cover fast and slow burns: 14.4/1h and 6/6h page, 1/3d tickets for a 99.9% SLO.
Trade-off: more rules to maintain; low-traffic services need minimum-request guards.
followups: What is the detection time for a 100% outage with the 14.4 rule?
How would you test these rules before trusting them?
