one: A practised way to handle outages (roles, communication, mitigation first) and to learn from them afterwards without blame.
an: A fire brigade drill: one commander, clear roles, put the fire out first, investigate the cause after.
how: Roles: incident commander (coordinates, decides), operations (hands on keyboard), communications (status page, stakeholders).
Mitigate before diagnosing: roll back, flip the flag, fail over, scale up. Root cause can wait until users are OK.
Blameless postmortem: timeline, impact, contributing factors, what went well, action items with owners. Ask "how did the system allow this?" not "who did this?".
Measure: time to detect (start of impact → alert), time to mitigate (alert → users OK). Say which one you mean: “MTTR” is used for repair, recovery, restore and resolve, which are different clocks.
why: Leads run incidents and own the follow-up. Blame makes people hide mistakes, which means the system never improves.
trade: Postmortems with no completed action items are theatre. Track them like any other work.

myth.m: The root cause was human error.
myth.r: Humans always err. The real question is why one mistake could take production down: missing guardrails, tests, or review.

q.s: Production is down right after a deploy. You suspect, but have not proven, the deploy caused it. First move?
o: Debug the code to find the exact bug
Roll back (mitigate), then investigate
Write the postmortem
Wait for more data
q.e: Restore service first. A rollback is cheap and reversible; prolonged downtime is not.

more: Severity levels and declaring an incident
lab: Write a blameless postmortem for a real past outage or bug in one of your projects using the template: summary, impact, timeline, contributing factors, what went well, action items with owners.
Run a 30-minute tabletop exercise with a friend: they break something; you play incident commander.

plain:
An incident is when production is broken for users. Good teams handle incidents with clear roles and one priority: restore service first, find the root cause later.

Afterwards they write a blameless postmortem: what happened, why the system allowed it, and what will change, without blaming a person.
bridge: If you have ever deployed something that broke the site, the right first move was always “roll back”, not “debug in production while users wait”. That instinct is the core of incident response.

walk.title: A 20-minute incident, handled well
steps: 14:02 Alert: checkout errors at 30%. On-call declares an incident and becomes incident commander.
14:04 Commander asks: what changed? A deploy went out at 13:58.
14:06 Decision: roll back first, investigate later. Rollback starts.
14:11 Errors back to normal. Status page updated: “resolved, monitoring”.
Next day: postmortem. Cause: a config value missing in one region. Actions: validate config at startup (owner: Aziz, due Friday), add a canary step.

terms: The person coordinating the response and making decisions.
Anything that stops user impact (rollback, flag off, failover).
A written review after an incident.
Focusing on system gaps, not on who made the mistake.
“Mean time to repair / recover / restore / resolve”: different teams mean different clocks, so always say which start and end points you measure.
Time to detect / time to mitigate
Start of impact → alert or report; alert → users are fine again. Splitting them shows where to invest.
insights: Practise before the real one. A 30-minute tabletop exercise quickly shows who does not know how to roll back.
Declare early. Downgrading an incident later costs nothing; declaring it late costs user trust.
Build the postmortem timeline from the incident channel while it is fresh. Memory of the order of events is wrong within days.

prod.summary: In production, incident response is a process you practise before you need it: clear severity levels, one commander, one channel, regular status updates, and a bias to mitigate (roll back, disable the flag, fail over) within minutes. Leads own the follow-up: a blameless postmortem whose action items are tracked to completion.
checklist: Severity levels are written down with examples (SEV1: checkout down for everyone; SEV3: one admin page broken) and say who must be paged.
Anyone can declare an incident without permission, and declaring and downgrading is cheap.
One incident channel, one commander. The commander coordinates and does not debug.
Status updates go out on a fixed rhythm (for example every 30 minutes for SEV1), even when the update is “no change, still investigating”.
Rollback and feature-flag kill switches are tested and take minutes, not a full CI pipeline.
A postmortem is required above a set severity, written within a few days, reviewed, and blameless in wording.
Action items have owners and due dates in the normal backlog, and someone reviews their completion rate.
numbers: Google SRE book postmortem triggers include user-visible downtime or degradation beyond a threshold, any data loss, and on-call intervention such as a rollback or traffic reroute.
PagerDuty's incident response guide defines SEV-1 to SEV-5, with SEV-1 and SEV-2 treated as major incidents that need an incident commander.
failures: Twenty people join the call, three of them try different fixes at the same time, and the outage gets worse.
Cause: no incident commander and no single decision-maker. Fix: name an IC in the first minutes; changes to production go through the IC; others observe or work assigned tasks.
The team spends 50 minutes finding the exact bug while checkout is down; a rollback would have taken 4 minutes.
Cause: diagnosing before mitigating. Fix: the first question is “what changed?”; if a recent deploy or flag is suspect, roll it back first.
Support and customers hear nothing for an hour, then learn about the outage on social media.
Cause: no communications role. Fix: assign a comms lead, post to the status page early, update on a fixed schedule.
The same incident happens again three months later.
Cause: postmortem action items were written but never done. Fix: track them in the normal backlog with owners and dates; review open items in a regular meeting.
Postmortems become short and vague; people stop admitting mistakes.
Cause: blame in the past (names in the “root cause”, consequences for the person). Fix: describe actions and system gaps, not people; leaders model this publicly.

code.title: Status update template the comms lead posts on a fixed rhythm
code.src:
[SEV1] Checkout errors — update 3 (14:40 UTC)

Impact:    ~30% of checkout attempts fail with an error page.
           Browsing and login are not affected.
Started:   14:02 UTC
Status:    Mitigating. Deploy 2026-10-02.3 is being rolled back.
Next step: Confirm error rate returns below 0.1% after rollback.
Next update: 15:10 UTC, or sooner if status changes.

IC: Dilnoza   Ops: Aziz   Comms: Kamola   Channel: #inc-checkout
code.note: Users and support need impact, status and the time of the next update more than technical detail. “Next update” is a promise: keep it even if nothing changed.

qs.s: During a SEV1, the incident commander, who is also the strongest engineer, starts reading code to find the bug. Nobody is updating the status page or deciding between rollback and failover. What should happen?
o: Nothing: the strongest engineer should debug
Wait until the bug is found, then assign roles
The IC hands debugging to someone else and goes back to coordinating, deciding and keeping comms on schedule
Everyone should start debugging in parallel
qs.e: An IC who debugs stops coordinating. The role is to decide, assign and communicate. Mitigation decisions and updates stall without it.

qs.s: A postmortem lists the root cause as: “Engineer X ran a migration without testing.” As the lead reviewing it, what change do you ask for?
o: Add a note that Engineer X has been warned
Delete the postmortem, because it was a single mistake
Add a second root cause: QA failed too
Rewrite it to ask why the system let an untested migration reach production (no CI check, no review, no staging run) and add actions for those gaps
qs.e: Blaming one person does not prevent the next mistake. The useful findings are the missing guardrails, and fixing them protects against every engineer making the same error.

qs.s: Your dashboard says “MTTR: 45 minutes”. The CTO wants it halved. Before acting, what do you check first?
o: Which clock it measures (detect, mitigate or fully resolve) and where the time goes: if detection takes 30 of the 45 minutes, better alerting helps more than faster fixes
How many engineers were on call
Whether the average should be replaced by the maximum
How many postmortems were written
qs.e: “MTTR” is ambiguous and an average hides the shape. Splitting time to detect from time to mitigate shows which investment actually reduces user impact.

qs.s: Read the incident timeline. To reduce user impact next time, where is the biggest improvement?

code.title: Timeline (UTC)
code.src:
09:12  Deploy 2026-10-02.4 rolls out
09:14  Checkout error rate rises from 0.1% to 9%
09:41  First customer complaint on social media
09:47  Alert fires (threshold: 10% errors for 30 min)
09:52  Incident declared, IC assigned
10:01  Rollback complete
10:03  Error rate back to 0.1%
11:30  Root cause found: missing config key in one region

o: Faster rollbacks: 10:01 → 10:03 took too long
Root cause analysis: 87 minutes is too slow
Declaring incidents faster after the alert
Detection: impact started 09:14 but the alert fired at 09:47 (33 minutes) because the threshold was too high and too slow; a burn-rate alert would have paged within minutes
qs.e: Time to detect was 33 minutes; time to mitigate after the alert was 16. Root cause time does not affect users once they are fine. 9% errors on a 99.9% SLO is a burn rate of 90, which a 14.4 fast-burn rule catches within a few minutes.

qs.s: Read the postmortem action items. Which one should the lead push back on?

code.title: Postmortem: action items
code.src:
1. Validate required config keys at startup; fail readiness if missing   (owner: Aziz, due 10-09)
2. Add a 10% canary stage with automatic rollback on error rate          (owner: Kamola, due 10-16)
3. Engineers must be more careful when editing regional config          (owner: team)
4. Replace the 10%/30min error alert with SLO burn-rate alerts           (owner: Dilnoza, due 10-12)

o: Item 1, because startup checks slow down deploys
Item 3: it has no concrete change, no single owner and no date, and “be more careful” does not prevent the next mistake
Item 2, because canaries are only for large companies
Item 4, because alerting is not part of the root cause
qs.e: Good action items change the system and can be checked as done. “Be more careful” is blame in polite words. Item 4 matters: slow detection made the impact three times longer, and contributing factors are in scope, not only the trigger.

qs.s: During a SEV1, a VP joins the incident call and asks each engineer for a detailed status every few minutes. Mitigation is slowing down. What should the incident commander do?
o: Ask the engineers to answer quickly and keep going
Politely route stakeholder questions to the comms lead and a separate stakeholder channel with regular updates, and keep the working channel for responders
End the call and continue in private messages
Pause mitigation until the VP is fully briefed
qs.e: The IC protects the responders' focus. Stakeholders get information on a fixed rhythm from the comms role, which also keeps them from interrupting. Private messages lose the shared timeline that the postmortem depends on.

qs.s: A deploy that broke checkout also ran a migration that dropped the column orders.discount_code. Rolling back the app now fails because the old code reads that column. What is the key postmortem action?
o: Never run migrations
Always restore the database from backup before rolling back
Use expand/contract migrations: add new structures first, deploy code that no longer uses the old column, and drop it only in a later release, so any app version can be rolled back safely
Run migrations manually at night
qs.e: Rollback is the main mitigation tool, and a destructive migration in the same release removes it. Expand/contract keeps the old and new code compatible with the schema. A full restore loses all writes since the backup and is much slower than a rollback.

interview.q: Tell me about an incident you handled. What did you do, and what changed afterwards?
answer: Structure the story: impact (who, how many, how long), detection, roles, mitigation, communication, follow-up.
Show mitigation before diagnosis: what changed, the rollback or flag decision, and when users were fine.
Give numbers: time to detect, time to mitigate, budget spent, customers affected.
Describe system-level fixes, not people: guardrails, alerts, tests, runbooks, and whether they were finished.
Be honest about what went badly and what you would do differently; interviewers check for ownership without blame.
followups: What would you do differently as incident commander?
How did you know the action items actually reduced risk?

interview.q: How do you run a blameless postmortem when someone clearly made a mistake?
answer: Blameless does not mean nobody did anything; it means asking why the action made sense to them at the time and why the system allowed it to hurt users.
Describe actions without names in the analysis (“a migration was run”), and get the person's account first, privately if needed.
Find the missing guardrails: review, CI checks, staging, permissions, canary, alerting.
Action items change the system, have one owner and a date, and are tracked to completion.
Leaders model it: share their own mistakes, and never use postmortems in performance reviews.
followups: What if the same person causes three incidents?
How do you handle a postmortem that crosses team boundaries?

interview.q: How do you define severity levels, and when should someone declare an incident?
answer: Severity by user and business impact, with examples: SEV1 = core journey down for many users or data loss; SEV3 = minor feature broken with a workaround.
Each level says who is paged, whether an IC and comms lead are needed, update frequency and whether a postmortem is required.
Anyone may declare; declaring is cheap and downgrading is normal. Late declaration is the common failure.
Declare early when impact is unclear but growing; it is easier to stand down than to catch up.
Review severity after the fact to calibrate the definitions.
followups: Is a security breach with no visible downtime a SEV1?
How do you avoid incident fatigue from too many declarations?

one: Endpoints that tell load balancers and orchestrators whether an instance is alive and ready to serve.
an: A shop's OPEN/CLOSED sign. Liveness asks "is anyone inside?"; readiness asks "can they serve customers right now?".
how: Liveness: the process is not stuck. Keep it trivial; failing it triggers a restart.
Readiness: the instance can serve (warmed up, config loaded, critical dependencies reachable). Failing it removes the instance from traffic without restarting.
Startup probes give slow-booting apps time before liveness kicks in.
why: They make zero-downtime deploys and self-healing work. Wrong ones cause outages.
trade: Checking shared dependencies (DB) in liveness turns a DB blip into every instance restarting at once. Readiness can check dependencies, carefully.

myth.r: A good readiness check reflects whether the instance can actually do its job.

q.s: The DB has a 30-second failover. All app pods restart in a loop and the outage lasts 10 minutes. Likely culprit?
o: CDN
Liveness probes that check the database
DNS
Feature flags
q.e: Liveness should not depend on shared dependencies. Let readiness pull pods from rotation while the DB recovers.

more: Health checks during graceful shutdown (fail readiness first)
lab: Add /livez (process alive) and /readyz (DB reachable) to an API.
On SIGTERM, make /readyz return 503, wait a few seconds, finish in-flight requests, then exit. Verify with a load test during a restart.
docs: Kubernetes: Liveness, readiness and startup probes

plain: A health check is an endpoint the platform calls regularly to ask your app “are you OK?”. There are two kinds of question. Liveness: are you stuck? If not alive, the platform restarts you. Readiness: can you handle traffic right now? If not ready, the platform stops sending you requests, but does not restart you.
bridge: Netlify and Vercel do this invisibly. On container platforms and Kubernetes you write the endpoints yourself, often called /livez (liveness) and /readyz (readiness).

walk.title: How a bad health check made an outage worse
steps: The liveness check was written as “query the database; return 200 if it works”.
The managed database does a 30-second failover.
Every pod's liveness check fails at the same time. The platform restarts every pod.
Restarting pods all reconnect at once and are slow to start; the app is down for 10 minutes instead of 30 seconds.
Fix: liveness checks only that the process responds. Readiness may check the database, so pods stop receiving traffic during the failover without being restarted.

terms: Is the process stuck? Failing → restart.
Can it serve traffic now? Failing → no traffic, no restart.
Gives slow-starting apps time before liveness checks begin.
Finishing current requests before shutting down.
insights: Test probes under failure, not only on a healthy day: stop the database for 30 seconds in staging and watch which pods restart.
Watch the pod restart count. Restarts with no crash in the logs usually mean a failed liveness probe.
Probe settings are part of your contract with the platform. Review probe changes as carefully as code changes.

prod.summary: In production, health checks are the contract between your app and the platform (Kubernetes, ECS, an ALB). Seniors keep liveness cheap and local, let readiness reflect “can I serve right now”, and design shutdown so the instance leaves the load balancer before it stops accepting connections. Wrong probes do not just fail to help: they turn a small blip into a restart storm.
checklist: Liveness checks only the process (event loop responds). It never calls the database, cache or another service.
Readiness checks the minimum needed to serve, with a short timeout (well under the probe timeoutSeconds).
Slow-booting apps use a startupProbe instead of a large initialDelaySeconds on liveness.
On SIGTERM: readiness returns 503, the app keeps serving for a few seconds while endpoints update, finishes in-flight requests, then exits before terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
Probe timeouts match reality: the default timeoutSeconds is 1s, which a busy Node process under GC or CPU throttling can miss.
Health endpoints are cheap, unauthenticated, not logged on every call, and not exposed publicly with internal details.
You know what your load balancer does when all targets fail: an AWS ALB “fails open” and sends traffic to all of them anyway.
numbers: Kubernetes probe defaults: periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1, failureThreshold 3, successThreshold 1, initialDelaySeconds 0. So a dead container is restarted after about 30 seconds.
Kubernetes default terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30.
AWS ALB health check defaults (instance/ip targets): interval 30s, timeout 5s, unhealthy after 2 failures, healthy after 5 successes, success code 200, path /.
The native preStop: sleep hook is GA in Kubernetes 1.34 (beta and on by default since 1.30).
failures: Pods show CrashLoopBackOff and “Liveness probe failed” during a 30-second database failover; the outage lasts 10 minutes.
Cause: liveness checks the database, so every pod restarts at once and they all reconnect together. Fix: liveness checks the process only; readiness may check the DB.
Every deploy causes a few hundred 502s at the load balancer.

Cause: the pod exits on SIGTERM immediately, but endpoints/ALB still send it traffic for a few seconds. Fix: fail readiness and sleep 5–10s in preStop before shutting down, then drain in-flight requests.
Under load, healthy pods are randomly restarted; logs show “Liveness probe failed: context deadline exceeded”.

Cause: timeoutSeconds: 1 with CPU throttling or a blocked event loop. The restart moves load to other pods, which then fail too. Fix: raise the timeout, fix the blocking work, and set CPU requests correctly.
A Java/large Node app never becomes Running: killed during boot every time.
Cause: liveness starts before the app has finished starting. Fix: add a startupProbe with enough failureThreshold × periodSeconds to cover the slowest boot.
All instances report healthy, but users get errors on every request.

Cause: the health endpoint returns 200 from a static route and checks nothing the real requests need (config missing, migrations not applied). Fix: readiness checks what serving actually needs; alert on real request success, not probe status.

code.title: Kubernetes probes and graceful shutdown for an API container
code.src:
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/api:1.42.0
      ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
      startupProbe:            # up to 30 x 5s = 150s to boot
        httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 3000 }
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 30
      livenessProbe:           # process only: never the database
        httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 3000 }
        periodSeconds: 10
        timeoutSeconds: 3
        failureThreshold: 3
      readinessProbe:          # may check the DB with a short timeout
        httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 3000 }
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 2
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          sleep: { seconds: 5 }  # let endpoints drop the pod before SIGTERM
code.note: The preStop sleep runs before SIGTERM is sent and counts against the 30s grace period, so the app still needs to finish in-flight requests quickly after SIGTERM. The sleep action needs Kubernetes 1.30 or newer.

qs.s: Your probe uses Kubernetes defaults (periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3). The app's event loop freezes completely. Roughly how long until the kubelet restarts the container?
o: 1 second
10 seconds
5 minutes
About 30 seconds
qs.e: Three failed checks, 10 seconds apart, plus up to a 1s timeout each: about 30 seconds. That is also the minimum time a stuck pod keeps getting traffic unless readiness fails sooner.

qs.s: A Node API's readiness check runs SELECT 1 against Postgres with no timeout. The DB becomes slow (5s per query). What happens?
o: Nothing: readiness never affects traffic
Readiness times out on every pod at once, all pods become NotReady, and the Service has zero endpoints: a full outage even for routes that do not need the DB
All pods restart in a loop
Kubernetes automatically increases the probe timeout
qs.e: Readiness failures on every pod remove every endpoint. Readiness can check dependencies, but think about what failing everywhere at once means; some teams only check local state and let requests fail fast instead.

qs.s: Every rolling deploy produces a burst of 502 errors at the ingress, even though new pods are ready. Which change most directly fixes it?
o: Add a short preStop sleep and drain in-flight requests after SIGTERM, so old pods leave the endpoints before they stop
Make the liveness probe check the database
Set initialDelaySeconds: 60 on readiness
Lower terminationGracePeriodSeconds to 5
qs.e: Endpoint removal is asynchronous; the ingress keeps routing to an old pod for a moment after SIGTERM. Waiting a few seconds and draining closes that gap. A shorter grace period makes it worse.

qs.s: Review this code. Kubernetes uses /livez as the liveness probe. What happens during a 40-second database failover?

code.title: health.ts

o: Every pod fails liveness at the same time and is restarted; all pods reconnect together and the outage lasts much longer than the failover
Pods are removed from the Service until the DB is back, then return
Nothing, because liveness only matters during startup
Only the pod that sent the query is restarted
qs.e: Liveness failure means “restart me”. A shared dependency makes every pod fail together. “Removed from the Service until the DB is back” describes readiness, which is where a careful dependency check belongs. Liveness should test only the process (for example, that the event loop answers).

qs.s: This shutdown code runs on every deploy. The ingress shows a burst of 502s each time. What is wrong?

code.title: server.ts

o: server.close() must be awaited with await because it returns a promise
SIGTERM is never sent by Kubernetes

The process exits at once: in-flight requests are cut, and the pod is still in the endpoints for a few seconds. Fail readiness, keep serving briefly (or use a preStop sleep), call server.close(cb) and exit in the callback
Port 3000 is not allowed in Kubernetes
qs.e: process.exit(0) runs right after close() starts, so open requests never finish. Endpoint removal is asynchronous, so new requests still arrive. server.close takes a callback; it does not return a promise. Since Node 19, server.close() also closes idle keep-alive connections, so with the callback version the process exits as soon as the last in-flight response is sent.

qs.s: Read the pod events. The app needs about 70 seconds to load its model at boot. What is the right fix?

code.title: kubectl describe pod api-7c9f
code.src:
startupProbe:  http-get :3000/livez  period=10s  timeout=1s  failure=3

Events:
  Warning  Unhealthy  31s  kubelet  Startup probe failed: connection refused
  Warning  Unhealthy  21s  kubelet  Startup probe failed: connection refused
  Warning  Unhealthy  11s  kubelet  Startup probe failed: connection refused
  Normal   Killing    11s  kubelet  Container api failed startup probe, will be restarted

o: Remove the startup probe and add initialDelaySeconds: 70 to readiness
Increase timeoutSeconds to 70
Raise failureThreshold so that failureThreshold × periodSeconds covers the slowest boot with margin, for example 12 × 10s = 120s
Make the liveness probe call the model to check it is loaded
qs.e: The startup probe allows 3 × 10s = 30s, but boot takes 70s, so the pod is killed every time and never starts. The timeout is per check, not total. Liveness and readiness do not run until the startup probe succeeds, so a long startup budget does not slow down failure detection later.

qs.s: All targets behind an AWS Application Load Balancer fail their health checks at the same time (a bad readiness check after a deploy). What does the ALB do?
o: Returns 503 to every client until a target is healthy
Fails open: it routes requests to all targets anyway, as if they were healthy
Routes traffic to the previous deployment
Stops accepting TCP connections
qs.e: AWS documents that when a target group has only unhealthy targets, the ALB sends requests to all of them. This protects you from a health check bug taking everything down, but it also means “all unhealthy” is not the same as “no traffic”. Know this before you design deep health checks.

interview.q: Design health checks for a Node API running in Kubernetes behind an ingress.
answer: Liveness: process-only, cheap, no dependencies; answer from the event loop. Failure = restart.
Readiness: can this pod serve now? Config loaded, warm-up done, connection pool usable; short timeouts; think about what happens if every pod fails it at once.
Startup probe for slow boots, sized as failureThreshold × periodSeconds above the slowest boot.
Timeouts realistic for a busy process (the 1 s default is tight under GC or CPU throttling).
Probes are not logged per call, not public, and do not leak internals; a separate /status page for humans can be detailed.
Alert on real request success, not on probe status.
followups: Should readiness check the database? What are the arguments both ways?
How do you detect a stuck event loop?

interview.q: Walk me through what happens when a pod is terminated during a rolling deploy, and how you get zero dropped requests.
answer: The pod is marked terminating; in parallel, the endpoints controller removes it and kube-proxy/ingress update over the next seconds.
The preStop hook runs first (for example a 5–10 s sleep) so routing catches up before the app stops listening.
Then SIGTERM: the app stops accepting new connections, finishes in-flight requests, closes idle keep-alive connections, flushes telemetry, exits.
All of it must fit inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 s), otherwise SIGKILL.
Rolling update settings (maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge) and readiness of new pods make sure capacity never drops.
followups: What changes for long-lived connections like WebSockets?
Why can the app not simply rely on readiness failing after SIGTERM?

interview.q: Should a readiness check include downstream dependencies like the database or another service?
answer: Including a dependency means every pod fails together when it is down: zero endpoints, and even routes that do not need it fail.
Excluding it means pods take traffic and return errors fast, which may be better: clear 503s, circuit breakers, degraded responses.
Middle ground: check only hard local requirements (pool initialised, config loaded) and use timeouts and breakers for dependencies at request time.
Never call other services from liveness; avoid chains where A's readiness depends on B's readiness.
Remember the load balancer's behaviour when all targets are unhealthy (ALB fails open).
followups: How would you show a degraded state to users?
What does a cascading readiness failure look like in metrics?

one: RPO: how much data you can afford to lose. RTO: how long you can afford to be down. Backups exist to meet both, and only count if restores are tested.
an: RPO is how many pages of your thesis you would lose if the laptop died now. RTO is how long until you are writing again on a new laptop.
how: Nightly snapshots → RPO up to 24h. Point-in-time recovery (continuous WAL archiving) → RPO of minutes or seconds.
Keep backups in another account or region, so one compromised account or region cannot delete everything.
Test restores on a schedule. An untested backup is a hope, not a backup.
why: Ransomware, a bad migration, an accidental DELETE without WHERE: replicas copy all of these instantly. Only backups bring data back.
trade: Lower RPO/RTO costs more. Agree targets with the business per system.

myth.m: We are on a managed DB, so backups are handled.
myth.r: Check retention, whether PITR is enabled, and whether anyone has ever restored one. Deleting the instance can delete its automated backups too.

q.s: At 14:05 a script deleted most rows in the orders table. You have nightly backups (02:00) and PITR enabled. Best restore target?
o: Last night's 02:00 snapshot
Point-in-time restore to 14:04 into a new instance, then copy the lost rows back
Restore from a read replica
Ask users to re-enter orders
q.e: PITR minimises loss. Restoring to a separate instance avoids destroying the morning's legitimate writes.

more: Restore drills and measuring actual RTO
lab: Take a pg_dump of a local database, drop it, and restore it. Time it.
On a managed provider you use (Supabase, Neon, RDS), find the backup retention and PITR settings and write them down.
Write a one-page restore runbook and actually follow it once.

plain:
Backups exist to get data back after something goes wrong: a bad script deletes rows, ransomware encrypts the server, a region fails.

Two numbers define what you need. RPO: how much recent data you can afford to lose (last hour? last minute?). RTO: how long you can afford to be down while restoring. A backup you have never restored is only a hope.
bridge: Git is a backup system for code with RPO = your last push. Your database needs the same level of care, and it is not automatic just because you use a managed service.

walk.title: Recovering from an accidental delete
steps: 14:05: a script with a bug deletes 90% of the orders table.
Nightly backups exist (02:00), but restoring them would lose 12 hours of orders.
Point-in-time recovery is enabled. You restore the database to 14:04 into a new instance (not over production).
You copy the deleted rows from the restored instance back into production.
Afterwards: restrict who can run scripts on production, require a review, and practise restores monthly.

terms: Recovery point objective: maximum acceptable data loss.
Recovery time objective: maximum acceptable downtime.
Restoring the database to any moment, using continuous logs.
Practising a restore to prove it works.
insights: The only proof that a backup works is a recent restore. Show the date of the last drill and its measured restore time on a dashboard.
Replicas are not backups: they copy a DELETE to every node within seconds.
In an emergency, restore into a new instance first. Restoring over production can destroy more data and the evidence of what happened.

prod.summary: In production, a backup strategy is judged by one thing: the last time someone restored it, how long it took, and how much data was missing. Seniors set RPO/RTO per system with the business, turn on point-in-time recovery for primary databases, keep a copy outside the main account, and run restore drills that measure real RTO.
checklist: PITR (continuous WAL archiving) is enabled on every primary database, and the retention period is written down (for example RDS 7 or 35 days).

At least one backup copy lives in a different account or region, with separate credentials and, ideally, immutability (S3 Object Lock, vault lock), so ransomware or a leaked admin key cannot delete it.
Deletion protection is on, and the team knows what happens to automated backups when an instance is deleted.
A scheduled restore drill restores into a fresh instance, runs sanity queries (row counts, latest created_at), and records the time taken as the real RTO.
Backups are monitored: an alert fires if the newest backup or the newest archived WAL file is older than expected.
Non-database state is covered too: object storage (versioning), secrets, config, and the infrastructure code needed to rebuild the stack.
Backups are encrypted, and the encryption keys are themselves recoverable (a lost KMS key makes the backup useless).
numbers: Amazon RDS backup retention: 0–35 days (0 disables automated backups). Default is 7 days from the console and 1 day from the API/CLI.
Amazon RDS: if you delete an instance without “retain automated backups”, automated backups in the same region are deleted and cannot be recovered. Manual snapshots are kept.

PostgreSQL defaults: archive_mode = off, archive_timeout = 0. The docs call an archive_timeout of about a minute “usually reasonable”; each forced switch still writes a full WAL segment (16 MB by default).
Nightly-only backups mean an RPO of up to 24 hours.
failures: During a restore you discover the dumps from the last three weeks are 0 bytes.
Cause: the backup job failed silently (expired credentials, disk full) and nobody checked the output. Fix: alert on backup age and size, and verify each backup by restoring it automatically.
A restore of a 2 TB database takes 9 hours; the business expected 1 hour.

Cause: RTO was assumed, never measured. Logical dumps (pg_restore) rebuild indexes and are slow at this size. Fix: measure RTO in drills; use physical/snapshot restores for large databases, or keep a warm standby when RTO must be short.
An attacker with an admin key deletes the database, its snapshots and the backup bucket.
Cause: all copies were in one account with one set of credentials. Fix: copy backups to a separate account with write-only access from production, and use object lock or vault lock retention.
After a bad migration you restore last night's snapshot over production and lose 12 hours of orders.
Cause: restored in place, without PITR. Fix: always restore into a new instance, use PITR to the minute before the mistake, then copy the needed rows back.
The restore works, but the app cannot read the data: “could not decrypt”.

Cause: the KMS key or the application-level encryption key was deleted or rotated without keeping old versions. Fix: back up and protect keys with the same care as data, and include decryption in the drill.

code.title: A small restore drill that measures real RTO
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
DRILL_DB="drill_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M)"   # one name, even if the drill crosses midnight

# 1. Custom-format dump (parallel restore needs -Fc or -Fd)
pg_dump --format=custom --no-owner "$PROD_URL" > /backups/app.dump

# 2. Restore into a fresh, throwaway database, never over production
start=$(date +%s)
createdb -h "$DRILL_HOST" "$DRILL_DB"
pg_restore --jobs=4 --no-owner --exit-on-error -h "$DRILL_HOST" -d "$DRILL_DB" /backups/app.dump
end=$(date +%s)

# 3. Prove the data is real, not just that the command exited 0
psql -h "$DRILL_HOST" -d "$DRILL_DB" -Atc \
  "select count(*), max(created_at) from orders"

echo "restore took $((end - start))s"   # measured restore time for this size
dropdb -h "$DRILL_HOST" "$DRILL_DB"
code.note: The sanity query is the important line: a restore that “succeeds” into an empty table is the classic silent failure. --exit-on-error makes pg_restore stop on the first error instead of reporting errors only at the end. For large databases, practise the snapshot/PITR restore you would really use.

qs.s: The business says: “We can lose at most 5 minutes of orders, and must be back within 1 hour.” You have nightly pg_dump backups only. Which statement is true?
o: Both targets are met, because pg_dump is consistent
RTO is met but RPO is not
RPO is not met (it is up to 24h); you need PITR/WAL archiving, and RTO is unknown until you time a restore
RPO is met, because replicas exist
qs.e: Nightly dumps give an RPO of up to a day. RTO depends on data size and restore method and must be measured, not assumed.

qs.s: Ransomware gets the AWS admin keys of your production account. Which backup setup survives?
o: Snapshots copied to a separate backup account that production can write to but not delete from, with object lock / vault lock retention
Automated RDS snapshots with 35-day retention in the same account
A read replica in another region
Nightly dumps in an S3 bucket in the same account with versioning
qs.e: An attacker with admin rights in the same account can delete snapshots, replicas and versioned objects. Only a separate trust boundary plus immutability protects you.

qs.s: You need to recover rows deleted by a bad script at 14:05. Where should you run the point-in-time restore?
o: Over the production instance, to save time
Into a new instance at 14:04, then copy the deleted rows back to production
Into a read replica, then promote it
Into staging, then point production traffic at staging
qs.e: Restoring in place would erase all valid writes after 14:04. A side restore lets you copy back only what was lost. A replica already contains the deletion.

qs.s: This nightly backup ran green for weeks. During a restore, the files turn out to be about 20 bytes each. Find the bug.

code.title: backup.sh (cron, 02:00)
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
pg_dump "$DATABASE_URL" | gzip > "/backups/db-$(date +%F).sql.gz"
aws s3 cp "/backups/db-$(date +%F).sql.gz" s3://acme-backups/
echo "backup ok"

o: gzip corrupts SQL dumps
Without set -o pipefail, the pipeline's exit code is gzip's; when pg_dump fails (for example expired password), gzip still writes an empty archive and the script reports success
date +%F is not valid in cron
aws s3 cp truncates files over 5 GB
qs.e: An empty input compressed by gzip is about 20 bytes, and gzip exits 0. set -e only sees the last command of a pipeline. Add set -o pipefail, and also check backup size and age from monitoring, because scripts fail in other silent ways too.

qs.s: These lines repeat in the PostgreSQL log for two days, and disk usage of pg_wal keeps growing. What happens if nobody acts?

code.title: postgresql.log
code.src:
LOG:  archive command failed with exit code 1
DETAIL:  The failed archive command was: aws s3 cp pg_wal/000000010000003A000000F2 s3://wal-archive/...
WARNING:  archiving write-ahead log file "000000010000003A000000F2" failed too many times, will try again later

o: PostgreSQL deletes the old WAL files, so only PITR is affected
Nothing serious; archiving is optional once it has failed
Replication stops, but the primary keeps running normally forever
WAL files cannot be removed until archived, so pg_wal fills the disk and PostgreSQL does a PANIC shutdown; meanwhile your real PITR point is stuck two days in the past
qs.e: PostgreSQL keeps every WAL segment until archive_command succeeds, so a broken archive is both a data-protection gap (RPO grows every minute) and an availability risk. The docs describe the PANIC shutdown when the disk fills. Alert on archiver failures (pg_stat_archiver.failed_count, last_archived_time).

qs.s: Restore drill: a 400 GB Postgres database takes 6 hours to restore with pg_restore, mostly rebuilding indexes. The business RTO is 1 hour. Which change can actually meet it?
o: Physical recovery: storage snapshots or a physical backup tool (base backup plus WAL replay), or a warm standby you can promote, then measure it in a drill
Compress the dump more strongly
Run pg_dump twice a day instead of once
Raise --jobs from 4 to 64 and expect a 16x speed-up
qs.e: Logical restore replays SQL and rebuilds every index, so time grows with data size. Physical restores copy data files and replay only recent WAL. More parallel jobs help up to the number of large tables and CPU/disk limits, not linearly. Dumping more often improves RPO, not RTO.

qs.s: A buggy cleanup script deleted 50,000 objects from an S3 bucket that has versioning on. A lifecycle rule expires noncurrent versions after 30 days. The script ran 2 days ago. Can you recover?
o: No, deleted objects in S3 are gone
Only from the last AWS-managed backup of S3
Only if MFA delete was enabled
Yes: a plain delete only adds a delete marker; removing the markers (or copying the previous versions back) restores the objects, as long as the lifecycle rule has not yet expired those versions
qs.e: With versioning, a delete without a version ID creates a delete marker and the data becomes a noncurrent version. The 30-day lifecycle rule gives you a deadline. S3 has no automatic backup of its own unless you set up AWS Backup or replication; MFA delete only protects against permanent version deletion.

interview.q: Design backup and recovery for a Postgres-backed SaaS product.
answer: Agree RPO/RTO per data store with the business; the primary DB usually needs minutes of RPO, so PITR (continuous WAL archiving or the managed equivalent) is on.
Copies outside the main trust boundary: a separate account with write-only access from production and immutability (Object Lock or vault lock).
Cover everything needed to rebuild: object storage with versioning, secrets and keys (recoverable KMS keys), infrastructure as code, configuration.
Monitor backups: newest backup age and size, WAL archiver failures, alert when stale.
Scheduled restore drills into a fresh instance, with sanity queries and measured restore time; a written runbook.
Trade-off: lower RPO/RTO costs more (standbys, cross-region copies); pick per system, not one level for everything.
followups: How would your design change for 5 TB?
How do you handle a user's deletion request when backups are immutable?

interview.q: We have a hot standby replica in another region. Do we still need backups?
answer: Yes. A replica protects against hardware or region loss (availability), with RPO equal to replication lag.
It copies every logical mistake instantly: a DELETE without WHERE, a bad migration, ransomware encryption done through the database.
Backups with PITR let you go back in time to just before the mistake; replicas cannot.
Replicas usually share credentials with production, so an attacker can delete them too.
Delayed replicas (for example 1 hour behind) are a middle ground but do not replace backups.
followups: What is the RPO of an asynchronous replica during a failover?
When would you use a delayed replica?

interview.q: How do you know your backups actually work?
answer: Only by restoring them: automated restores into a fresh instance on a schedule.
Validate data, not exit codes: row counts, latest timestamps, checksums of key tables, the application can start against it.
Measure and record restore time as the real RTO, and compare it with the target as data grows.
Monitor the backup pipeline itself: age, size trend, archiver failures, failed copies to the backup account.
Include the hard parts in drills: decryption keys, cross-account access, the person on call following the runbook.
followups: What signals would tell you a backup is silently broken?
How often should a full drill run?

Practice: the set -e script uploaded a 20-byte gzip and printed “backup ok”; a failing archive_command logged the exact lines and kept every WAL segment as .ready.
